analysis.one_liner: Creates a dedicated federal trust fund, paid for by a higher corporate tax rate, to fix and expand the nation's water and sewer systems.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote in the 115th Congress; no water trust fund was created and the corporate tax rate stayed at 21%.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a Water Affordability, Transparency, Equity, and Reliability Trust Fund, financed by raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5%. The fund — up to $34.85 billion a year — would pay for clean-water and drinking-water programs, lead pipe replacement, lead-free water in schools, septic system repairs, rural water wells, and grants to rural, small, and tribal communities. It also orders a study of water affordability and discrimination, lets public systems use federal money to buy private water utilities, and requires that funded projects use American-made materials and prevailing wages. It was referred to four House committees and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and communities struggling with water costs and contamination gain the most: people on failing septic systems, families with lead in school or home water pipes, rural residents without reliable wells, and tribal and small-town systems that need upgrades. Water and sewer construction workers also gain, since the bill requires prevailing wages and encourages project labor agreements. Low-income households facing shutoffs for unpaid bills gain from required affordability protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with unaffordable or unsafe water service

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated trust fund, automatically funded by the higher corporate tax, that sends money to state clean-water and drinking-water loan funds without needing a fresh vote in Congress each year.
Requires EPA grants to school districts to remove lead from school drinking water and to test for lead, directly protecting children.
Pays for homeowners to repair or replace failing septic systems, and permanently funds a program for household water wells in rural areas.
Expands aid to rural and small towns and tribal governments for water and sewer systems, and requires states to direct half their loan-fund subsidies to communities that need affordability help.
Orders a federal study of water affordability, water shutoffs, and discrimination in water service, and requires protections for households facing shutoff for unpaid bills.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations pay a higher tax rate (21% to 24.5%), a cost that falls partly on their shareholders and partly on workers through wages over time. Public water systems and states also take on new conditions, such as directing at least half of loan-fund subsidies to communities needing affordability help and using American-made materials.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations through a higher tax rate

drawbacks.text: It is funded by raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5%, a cost that economists say is borne partly by workers through lower wages and partly by shareholders — so the bill trades one household cost (water bills) for another (the broad cost of higher corporate taxes).

The bill requires public water systems to be publicly owned, operated, and managed as a condition of drinking-water funding, and authorizes buying private water utilities from a willing or unwilling seller — a significant shift that private water companies and some local officials would contest.
The trust fund is capped at $34.85 billion a year and funded by the new tax revenue, so if corporate tax receipts fall short of the cap, the guaranteed water spending shrinks with them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — dedicated federal money to fix and expand water and sewer systems, replace lead pipes, and protect school drinking water — addresses a real, widespread problem that households currently pay for through high bills or unsafe taps. The main cost is the financing: a 3.5-point corporate tax increase (about a 17% higher rate), which independent analysts would expect to fall partly on workers through lower wages and partly on shareholders. The bill spends at a very large annual scale without a hard needs assessment beyond its own cap, and critics of dedicated trust funds note they can reduce annual budget discipline. On balance, the public benefit is broad and the mechanism is straightforward, but the design leans heavily on one revenue source and the acquisition provisions deserve scrutiny.

outcome.mechanism: After its introduction in April 2018 it was referred to four House committees and two subcommittees, none of which acted, so it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 25, 2018 and referred to four committees — Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Agriculture — none of which reported it.
It was referred to subcommittees on Water Resources and Environment and on Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit in the weeks after introduction, and no further action was taken.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill expired without any vote in the House or Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No water trust fund was created, so households with unsafe or unaffordable water service gained nothing; taxpayers avoided the new corporate tax increase, and shareholders and private water companies avoided the tax and the public-ownership conditions.

for.name: Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its introduction with 35 original cosponsors.

for.name: 53 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 53 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House committee leadership (four committees)
against.role: Chairs of Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or advanced the bill after referral, leaving it to expire.

sides.party_line_note: All 53 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on; the bill died before any vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Water and sewer construction and engineering firms
industries.note: Up to $34.85 billion a year of federal money flows into pipes, plants, lead-line replacement, and well and septic work, much of it performed by construction contractors.
The bill makes public ownership a funding condition and lets communities buy private water systems even from an unwilling seller, reducing the scope for private water-company growth.
A 3.5-point corporate tax increase funds the program, reducing after-tax profits for shareholders across the economy.
Water projects funded under the bill must, to the maximum extent practicable, use project labor agreements, which favor unionized construction labor.
